# Minimum _s-t_ Cuts with Fewer Cut Queries

Yonggang Jiang<sup>∗</sup> Danupon Nanongkai<sup>†</sup> Pachara Sawettamalya<sup>‡</sup>

**Abstract**

We study the problem of computing a minimum _s-t_ cut in an unweighted, undirected graph via _cut queries_. In this model, the input graph is accessed through an oracle that, given a subset of vertices \(S\subseteq V\) , returns the size of the cut (_S,V_\\_S_).

This line of work was initiated by Rubinstein, Schramm, and Weinberg (ITCS 2018), who gave a randomized algorithm that computes a minimum _s-t_ cut using \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) queries, thereby showing that one can avoid spending \(\widetilde{\Theta}(n^2)\) queries required to learn the entire graph.<sup>1</sup> A recent result by Anand, Saranurak, and Wang (SODA 2025) also matched this upper bound via a deterministic algorithm based on blocking flows.

In this work, we present a new randomized algorithm that improves the cut-query complexity to \(\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})\). At the heart of our approach is a query-efficient subroutine that incrementally reveals the graph edge-by-edge while increasing the maximum _s-t_ flow in the learned subgraph at a rate faster than classical augmenting-path methods. Notably, our algorithm is simple, purely combinatorial, and can be naturally interpreted as a recursive greedy procedure.

As a further consequence, we obtain a _deterministic_ and _combinatorial_ two-party communication protocol for computing a minimum _s-t_ cut using \(\widetilde{O}(n^{11/7})\) bits of communication. This improves upon the previous best bound of \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\), which was obtained via reductions from the aforementioned cut-query algorithms. In parallel, it has been observed that an \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})\)-bit randomized protocol can be achieved via continuous optimization techniques; however, these methods are fundamentally different from our combinatorial approach.

## 1 Introduction

The _minimum s-t cut_ problem is a cornerstone of combinatorial optimization and graph algorithms. Formally, given an undirected, unweighted graph _G_=(_V,E_) on _n_ vertices, along with two distinguished terminals \(s,t\in V\) , the goal is to compute an _s-t_ cut of the vertex set--that is, a partition (_S,T_) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\in T\)--that minimizes the number of edges crossing the cut, i.e., the quantity \(|E(S,T)|:=|E\cap(S\times T)|\). In this work, we study the complexity of computing a minimum _s-t_ cut in two computational models that restrict access to the input graph.

### Cut-query.

In this setting, we may query an oracle with a partition (_S,T_) of _V_ (i.e. _a cut_) to obtain the cut value |_E(S,T_)|. Our goal is to compute a minimum _s-t_ cut of _G_ while minimizing the total number of queries made to the oracle. This problem was first introduced by the work of Rubinstein, Schramm, and Weinberg \[RSW18\] in an effort to study submodular function minimization problem.<sup>2</sup> While the "trivial" _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) queries suffices to _learn_ the whole undirected graph, the work of \[RSW18\] were the first to break this quadratic barrier via an \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\)-query algorithm utilizing the randomized construction of a cut sparsifier. More recently, Anand, Saranurak, and Wang \[ASW25\] developed a new deterministic algorithm, matching the same \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) query complexity. Notably, their approach is purely combinatorial via an implementation of Dinitz’s blocking flow algorithm \[Din70\], thereby is vastly different from the techniques deployed in \[RSW18\]. Nevertheless, both algorithms circumvent the necessity to learn the whole graph which information-theoretically require \(\widetilde{\Omega}(n^2)\) queries to the oracle when the graph is dense.

The works of Rubinstein, Schramm, and Weinberg \[RSW18\] and Anand, Saranurak, and Wang \[ASW25\] approach the _s-t_ minimum cut problem from two completely orthogonal perspectives; yet both arrive at algorithms with the same query complexity of \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\). This convergence naturally raises the question: _Do the current_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\)_-query upper bounds represent a latent barrier for computing a minimum s-t cut?_ In this work, we show that we can indeed go below this bound.

**Theorem 1.1** (Main result #1)**.** _There is a randomized algorithm that computes a minimum s-t cut of an undirected unweighted graph G. The algorithm always makes_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})\) _cut queries to G and succeeds with high probability._

In addition, our algorithm can be extended to enumerate _all_ minimum _s-t_ cuts within the same query complexity, although we do not make this extension explicit in our later analysis. We also highlight that our algorithms are simple, purely combinatorial, and can be naturally interpreted as a recursive greedy procedure.

### Two-player communication.

In this setting, input graph _G_=(_V,E_) is edge-partitioned across two players, namely Alice has _G<sub>A</sub>_=(_V,E<sub>A</sub>_), and Bob has _G<sub>B</sub>_=(_V,E<sub>B</sub>_), with \(E=E_A\cup E_B\). The players are allowed to exchange a sequence of messages (via a _protocol_) with the goal of computing a minimum _s-t_ cut of _G_ while minimizing the total amount of communication between the players.

In fact, any upper bound in the cut-query model translates to an upper bound in the communication setting, with an additional _O_(log_n_) factor. To see this, observe that any cut query can be simulated with _O_(log_n_) bits of communication: Alice locally computes |_E<sub>A</sub>(S,T_)| and sends the result to Bob, who then computes |_E<sub>B</sub>(S,T_)| and sends it back to Alice. The players can thus recover the cut value by computing |_E(S,T_)|=|_E<sub>A</sub>(S,T_)|+|_E<sub>B</sub>(S,T_)|. Since both |_E<sub>A</sub>(S,T_)| and<tbc>

|_E<sub>B</sub>(S,T_)| are bounded by _O(n_<sup>2</sup>), they can each be represented with _O_(log_n_) bits, making the communication cost per query _O_(log_n_).

As an immediate corollary, simulating the deterministic \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\)-query algorithm of Anand, Sara nurak, and Wang \[ASW25\] yields a deterministic communication protocol with total cost \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) bits. Furthermore, although the algorithm of Rubinstein, Schramm, and Weinberg \[RSW18\] is originally randomized in the cut-query setting, it can be derandomized in the communication model, resulting in the same \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) deterministic upper bound. To our knowledge, prior to this work, no subquadratic deterministic or combinatorial protocol for computing a minimum _s-t_ cut is known beyond simulating one of these cut-query algorithms.

As a by-product of Theorem 1.1, our \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.6})\)-query algorithm immediately yields a two-player communication protocol with total communication cost of \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.6})\) bits. Furthermore, through a careful implementation of our algorithm, we obtain a _deterministic_ communication protocol with the improved complexity of \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.58})\) bits. This modest improvement arises from exploiting some key distinctions between the two models, thereby allowing us to realize the power of communication setting more truly.

**Theorem 1.2** (Main result #2)**.** _There is a deterministic two-player communication protocol that computes a minimum s-t cut of an undirected unweighted graph G. The protocol uses_ \(\widetilde{O}(n\nu^{4/7})\) _bits of communication where_ \(\nu\) _denotes the value of G’s minimum s-t cut, and always succeeds._

In parallel, it is known in the literature that one can achieve an \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})\)-bit protocol via a randomized non-combinatorial approach based on continuous optimizations--e.g., as observed by \[GJ25\].<sup>3</sup> Nevertheless, our result of Theorem 1.2 serves as the first _deterministic_ and _combinatorial_ communication protocol for computing a minimum _s-t_ cut that surpasses the \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) bounds.

## 1.1 Related Works

Although not the focus of our work, we briefly highlight related results on the cut-query complexity of a closely related problem: computing a _global_ minimum cut. The seminal work of Rubinstein, Schramm, and Weinberg \[RSW18\] also initiated the study of this problem for undirected, unweighted graphs and gave a randomized \(\widetilde{O}(n)\)-query algorithm, which spurred a sequence of follow-up works. Apers et al. \[AEG+22\] subsequently removed all polylogarithmic factors, obtaining the first truly linear _O(n_)-query algorithm. More recently, Anand, Saranurak, and Wang \[ASW25\] developed the first _deterministic_ algorithm for this problem, using \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) queries via a novel expander decomposition technique. Kenneth-Mordoch and Krauthgamer \[KK25b\] explored round-query trade-offs and showed that a global minimum cut can be computed in only two rounds using \(\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3})\) queries. For weighted undirected graphs, Mukhopadhyay and Nanongkai \[MN20\] achieved a near-linear \(\widetilde{O}(n)\)- query upper bound. Finally, the algorithm of \[RSW18\] was shown to be implementable in the semi-streaming model using only two passes as observed by Assadi, Chen, and Khanna \[ACK19\], and was later simplified by Assadi and Dudeja \[AD21\].

### Connections to Submodular Function Minimization.

A set function \(f:2^{[n]}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is called _submodular_ if it satisfies a diminishing returns property: for every \(A\subseteq B\subseteq[n]\) and \(x\notin B\), it holds that \(f(A\cup\{x\})-f(A)\ge f(B\cup\{x\})-f(B)\). The goal of the submodular function minimization (SFM) problem is to find a minimizer of _f_, given query access to a value oracle, while minimizing the number of queries. After decades of work \[GLS81; Cun85; Que98; FI00; Iwa03; Vyg03; Orl07;<tbc>

<sup>3</sup>The existence of a \(\widetilde{O}(n^{1.5})\)-bit protocol was brought to our attention through private communication with experts in the area. To respect the double-blind reviewing policy, we refrain from disclosing their identities.

<tbc>IO09; LSW15; ALS20; Jia21\], the state-of-the-art upper bound is _O(n_<sup>2</sup>log_n_), due to Jiang \[Jia23\]. On the other hand, the current best deterministic lower bound remains at \(\Omega(n\mathrm{log}n)\), established by Chakrabarty, Graur, Jiang, and Sidford \[CGJS22\], following a sequence of earlier linear-query lower bounds \[Har08; CLSW17; GPRW20\]. We also highlight another recent work by Chakrabarty, Graur, Jiang, and Sidford \[CGJS23\] which investigates the parallel complexity of SFM and may be of independent interest.

There is a well-known connection between SFM and the problem of computing minimum cuts in graphs. In fact, the minimum cut function--whether global or _s-t_, weighted or unweighted, directed or undirected--forms a canonical example of a submodular function. This connection has long motivated efforts to reduce SFM to specific cut problems. As emphasized in Rubinstein, Schramm, and Weinberg \[RSW18\], one major motivation for studying the cut-query complexity of minimum cuts was to use them as a proxy for proving quadratic lower bounds for SFM.

However, this approach faces significant limitations. The randomized \(\widetilde{O}(n)\)-query algorithm of \[RSW18\] and the subsequent truly linear _O(n_)-query algorithm of Apers et al. \[AEG+22\] exclude any \(\omega(n)\) lower bound for SFM via reductions from minimum cuts in unweighted, undirected graphs. Similarly, the near-linear upper bound of Mukhopadhyay and Nanongkai \[MN20\] rules out \(\widetilde{\omega}(n)\) lower bounds from weighted graphs. Our own result (Theorem 1.1) also rules out \(\widetilde{\omega}(n^{8/5})\) lower bounds from minimum _s-t_ cuts in unweighted graphs. Nevertheless, even a modest improvement--say, proving an \(\Omega(n^{1.01})\) lower bound for SFM via minimum _s-t_ cuts--would be a notable breakthrough.

Perhaps the most promising path toward proving quadratic lower bounds for SFM lies in the minimum cut problems on _directed_ graphs. The common techniques and subroutines that apply to designing cut query algorithms in undirected graphs often break down in the directed setting. At the extreme, even learning the underlying graph is impossible with only cut-query access: if a directed graph contains a cycle, reversing the orientation of the cycle leaves all directed cut values unchanged, leaving the two graphs indistinguishable via any number of cut queries. To this end, while we cannot hope to recover the entire directed input graph using only cut queries, Cunningham \[Cun85\] observed that \(\widetilde{O}(n^2)\) queries suffice to compute minimum cuts in directed graphs, even when the graph is weighted. To the best of our knowledge, this quadratic upper bound has stood ever since, and not even the slightest improvement to an _n_<sup>2-_o_(1)</sup> upper bound is known.<sup>4</sup> Therefore, any progress--either an \(\omega(n)\)-query lower bound or an _o(n_<sup>2</sup>)-query upper bound--would represent a major advance.

## 1.2 Organization

The remainder of this work is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the notation used throughout the paper. Readers familiar with graph-theoretic concepts, the cut-query model, and the two-party communication model may skip directly to Section 3, where we provide a high-level overview and sketch the main ideas behind our algorithm. The implementation and analysis in the cut-query model are presented in a combination of Section 4 and Section 5. The implementation and analysis in the two-player communication model are deferred to Section C. We conclude with a discussion of open problems in Section 6. Finally, Section A and Section B contain the missing proofs from earlier sections.

<sup>4</sup>Even for _reachability_, perhaps the simplest problem in directed graphs, no subquadratic-query upper bound is known.

## 2 Notations and Preliminaries

In this section, we introduce the terminologies and computation models that will be used throughout the paper. Due to brevity, some of the proofs are deferred to Section A.

### Graph.

Let _G_=(_V,E_) denote a graph with a designated terminals _s_ and _t_. Unless stated otherwise, a graph is assumed to be undirected and unweighted. For two graphs _G_=(_V,E_) and \(G'=(V,E')\) on the same vertex set, we denote \(G\cup G'=(V,E\cup E')\) as the graph obtained by combining the edges of _G_ and \(G'\). We also write \(G\cup e\) for the addition of a single edge _e_ to _G_.

In this work, we also study graphs whose edge sets comprise both undirected unweighted edge (i.e. unit-weight) and directed weighted edges. We call a graph of this type a _mixed graph_, denoted by G=(_G,F_) where _G_ is undirected unweighted graph, and _F_ is a directed graph with bounded weights. For a directed edge, we write (_a,b_) to represent an edge from _a_ to _b_. For an undirected edge, we may write it as either (_a,b_) or (_b,a_) interchangeably, with no implied direction.

For a weighted graph _G_=(_V,E_), we denote \(w_G:E\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) as the weight function that maps an edge of _G_ to its positive integral weight. The total weight of any edge set \(E'\subseteq E\) is given by \(w_G(E'):=\sum_{e\in E^\prime} w_G(e)\). Also denote _w(G_) or |_G_| to be the total weight of edges in the graph.

Let _G_=(_V,E<sub>G</sub>_) and _H_=(_V,E<sub>H</sub>_) be two graphs on the same set of vertices which may be directed or weighted. We say _H_ is a _subgraph_ of _G_, denoted \(H\unknown G\), iff \(E_H\subseteq E_G\), and \(w_H(e)\le w_G(e)\) for any edge \(e\in E_H\). When both _G_ and _H_ are undirected unweighted, the second condition is not necessary.

For any graph _G_=(_V,E_) and \(U\subseteq V\) , denote _G_\[_U_\] to be an induced subgraph of _G_ on vertex set _U_. For a partition (_V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>z</sub>_) of _V_ , denote \(G\langle V_1,..,V_z\rangle\) to be a (weighted) graph over _z_ super- vertices resulted from contracting each vertex set _V<sub>i</sub>_ into one super-vertex. Equivalently, we can view \(G\langle V_1,..,V_z\rangle\) as _G_ with all edges within each _G_\[_V<sub>i</sub>_\] removed.

### Flow and Maximum Flow.

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a (possibly directed weighted) graph with a designated source _s_ and sink _t_. A _unit of s-t flow_ (or simply a _unit flow_) is a directed path from _s_ to _t_. We say a directed graph _F_ is a _flow graph of value f_ if and only if _F_ can be exactly partitioned into _f_ unit flows. We denote MaxFlow(_G_) as the value of _G_’s largest flow subgraph. When _G_ is undirected unweighted, MaxFlow(_G_) corresponds to the maximum number of edge-disjoint _s-t_ paths that can be packed into _G_.

**Lemma 2.1** (Lemma 5.4 of \[RSW18\])**.** _Let F_=(_V,E_) _be a non-circular flow graph of value f with n vertices. Let W be the maximum weight of edges in F. Then, we have_ \(w(F)\le O(n\sqrt{fW})\).

The following lemma bounds the number of edges in a flow graph.

**Lemma 2.2.** _Let F_=(_V,E_) _be a non-circular flow graph of value f with n vertices. Then, F contains_ \(|E|\le O(n\sqrt{f})\) _edges._

### Residual Graph.

Given an undirected unweighted graph _G_ and a flow subgraph \(F\unknown G\), the _residual graph_ of _G_ induced by _F_, denoted _G<sub>F</sub>_, is obtained by replacing each edge in _F_ with its reverse edge, assigned a weight of 2. Notably, _G<sub>F</sub>_ is a mixed graph consisting of the undirected unweighted part _G_\\_F_, and a directed weighted part which is a reversal of _F_ with weight 2 on each edge (see Figure 1 for an illustration).

**Proposition 2.3.** _For any graph G and a flow subgraph_ \(F\unknown G\)_, we have:_<tbc>

\(MaxFlow(F)+MaxFlow(G_F)=MaxFlow(G).\)

## Cut and Minimum Cut.

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a (possibly directed weighted) graph with a designated terminals _s_ and _t_. A _cut_ of _G_ is defined as a partition (_S,T_) of the vertex set _V_ . If \(s\in S\) and \(t\in T\), we say such cut is an _s-t cut_. An undirected/directed edge \((a,b)\in E\) is said to _cross_ the cut if \(a\in S\) and \(b\in T\). The set of edges crossing the cut (_S,T_) is denoted by _E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_). The _size_ of a cut (_S,T_) is defined as the cardinality of _E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_), given by |_E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_)|. The _value_ of a cut is the total weight of the edges crossing the cut, quantified as \(w_G(S,T)=\sum_{e\in E_G(S,T)}w_G(e)\). When _G_ is undirected and unweighted, we may write the cut value by _w<sub>G</sub>(S,T_) or |_E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_)|. For clarity, we reserve the notation of cut value |_E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_)| solely for the case that _G_ is undirected and unweighted. For the remaining cases, we write the cut value as _w<sub>G</sub>(S,T_).

The _minimum s-t cut value_ of _G_, denoted by MinCut(_G_), is the minimum value among all possible _s-t_ cuts. An _s-t_ cut that attain the minimum cut value is called a _minimum s-t cut_. A cut (not necessarily an _s-t_ cut) of smallest value is called a _global minimum cut_. The following theorem, established in \[FF56\], formalizes the duality between maximum flow and minimum cuts.

**Theorem 2.4** (Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem)**.** _For any graph G with a source s and sink t, the maximum value of an s-t flow equals the minimum value of an s-t cut, formally:_<tbc>

\(MaxFlow(G)=MinCut(G).\)

<tbc>Throughout this paper, we use \(\nu(G)\) to denote the value of the maximum _s-t_ flow and, equivalently, the value of the minimum _s-t_ cut in the graph _G_:

\(\nu(G):=MaxFlow(G)=MinCut(G).\)

More precisely, we define \(\nu_{s,t}(G)\) as the value of the minimum _s-t_ cut. Since we always fix a specific pair of terminals (_s,t_), we omit the subscripts and simply write \(\nu(G)\).

### _k_-Connected Component.

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be an undirected graph that can possibly be weighted. We say \(U\subseteq V\) is _k-connected component_ iff _G_\[_U_\] has _global_ min-cut of value at least _k_. The following lemma is known. For its proof, we refer readers to Lemma 3.8 of \[RSW18\].

**Lemma 2.5.** _Let G be an n-vertex undirected weighted graph with no k-connected components. Then, we have_ \(w(G)\le k(n-1)\).

## Cut Sparsifier.

Let _G_ be an undirected graph that may be weighted, and let \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\). We say an undirected weighted graph _H_ is an \(\varepsilon\)_-cut sparsifier_ of _G_ iff \(E(H)\subseteq E(G)\) and we have \((1-\varepsilon)\cdot w_G(S,T)\le w_H(S,T)\le(1+\varepsilon)\cdot w_G(S,T)\) for any cut (_S,T_).

It is widely known that for any \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), any graph _G_ has an \(\varepsilon\)-cut sparsifier with \(\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)\) edges. We state the version of sparsifer we need via the following theorem.

**Theorem 2.6.** _Let G be an unweighted undirected connected graph with n vertices and average degree d. Then, for any_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)_, there exists an_ \(\varepsilon\)_-cut sparsifier of G with_ \(O\left(\frac{nlog^2n}{\varepsilon^2}\right)\) _edges and weights bounded by_ \(O\left(\frac{\varepsilon^2d}{log^2n}\right)\).

We make several remarks. First, the theorem establishes an asymptotically optimal trade-off between the number of edges and the maximum weight of the sparsifier. To see this, let _G_ be a graph with _m_ edges. Any \(\varepsilon\)-cut sparsifier must have total weight at least \((1-\varepsilon)m=\Omega(m)\). Since our sparsifier contains \(O\left(\frac{nlog^2n}{\varepsilon^2}\right)\) edges, at least one edge must carry a weight \(\frac{\Omega(m)}{O\left(\frac{nlog^2n}{\varepsilon^2}\right)}=\Omega\left(\frac{\varepsilon^2d}{log^2n}\right)\), which matches our upper bound up to constant factors.

Second, for completeness, the proof of Theorem 2.6 is deferred to Section B. In fact, we prove a stronger statement for an extended notion known as a _spectral_ sparsifier. We emphasize that our proof does not claim novelty in technique. Many foundational results on sparsification are well established \[Kar99; BK15; FHHP19; SS11; ST11; BSS12; CGP+23; LWZ25\], and our argument merely follows prior approaches, such as that of \[CGP+23\]. However, to the best of our knowledge, previous work has not explicitly addressed bounding the maximum edge weight in sparsifiers. When bounds are provided, they are typically of order \(\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^2n)\). Our contribution lies in explicitly deriving _asymptotically optimal_ bounds on the maximum edge weight. This refinement turns out to be critical for our algorithmic applications.

## 2.1 Cut-Query Model

In this setting, an input graph _G_=(_V,E_) is hidden from us, and we are only allow to make _cut- queries_ to the graph. In particular, for each query we can specify a cut (_S,T_) to an oracle, and receives |_E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_)| in return. Our objective is to compute a task (in this case, a minimum _s-t_ cut) while minimizing the query complexity of our algorithm. Note that the only notion of cost here is the queries; thus, we can assume to have an unlimited local computation power.

Many fundamental tasks can be simulated efficiently via cut queries. For instance, we can find out if an edge (_a,b_) exists in the graph within _O_(1) queries, learn all the _m_ edges in the graph within _O(n+m_log_n_) queries, or uniformly sample an edge of the graph with an amortized cost of _O_(log_n_) queries. This random sampling primitive also opens up many doors of opportunity to the world of sequential algorithm. Perhaps one of the most insightful takeaways from \[RSW18\] is that we can obtain a cut sparsifier of _G_ within not-too-many cut queries to _G_, thereby enabling us to obtain a \((1\pm\varepsilon)\)-approximation of the _value_ of the minimum _s-t_ cut.

**Lemma 2.7** (Theorem 3.5 of \[RSW18\])**.** _For any_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)_, there is a randomized algorithm that computes an_ \(\varepsilon\)_-cut sparsifier of G with_ \(\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)\) _edges and maximum weight_ \(\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^2n)\)_. The algorithm uses_ \(\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)\) _cut queries to G and succeeds w.h.p._

**Corollary 2.8.** _For any_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)_, there is a randomized algorithm that computes f such that_ \((1-\varepsilon)\nu(G)\le f\le(1+\varepsilon)\nu(G)\)_. The algorithm uses_ \(\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)\) _cut queries to G and succeeds w.h.p._

Throughout this paper, we will utilize a more specific type of query to a graph _G_=(_V,E_) called the _find-edge query_ which can be simulated efficiently via cut queries.

**Definition 2.9** (Find-edge query)**.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be an underlying graph. A_ find-edge _query takes in as inputs disjoint sets_ \(A,B\subseteq V\) _, and outputs_ FindEdge(_A,B_) _which is either_ "NONE" _if_ \(E\cap(A\times B)=\emptyset\)_, or an edge_ \((a,b)\in E\cap(A\times B)\) _if otherwise._

**Proposition 2.10.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be an underlying graph. Then, for any disjoint sets_ \(A,B\subseteq V\) _, we can determine_ FindEdge(_A,B_) _using either_

• _O_(1) _cut queries to G if_ FindEdge(_A,B_) _outputs_ "NONE" _(i.e._ \(E\cap\left(A\times B\right)=\emptyset\)_), or_<tbc>

• _O_(log_n_) _cut queries to G if_ FindEdge(_A,B_) _outputs an edge_ \((a,b)\in E\cap\left(A\times B\right)\).

One of its abundant benefits of the find-edge queries is that it allows us to learn the (contracted) graphs with query complexity near-linear in the representation size of the graph.

**Lemma 2.11.** _Let_ (_V_<sub>1</sub>_,...,V<sub>z</sub>_) _be a partition of a vertex set of G_=(_V,E). Then, we can learn all edges of_ \(G\langle V_1,\dots,V_z\rangle\) _using_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(z+|G\langle V_1,\dots,V_z\rangle|\right)\) _cut queries._

### 2.2 Two-Party Communication Model

In this setting, an input graph _G_=(_V,E_) is edge-partitioned across two players, namely Alice has her private graph _G<sub>A</sub>_=(_V,E<sub>A</sub>_), and Bob has his private graph _G<sub>B</sub>_=(_V,E<sub>B</sub>_), with \(E=E_A\cup E_B\). The players’ objective is to collaboratively compute a joint task (in this case, a minimum _s-t_ cut) by exchanging a sequence of messages, known as a _protocol_, while minimizing the total amount of communication. Note that the only notion of cost here is the communication; thus, Alice and Bob can be assumed to have unlimited local computation power.

Within this communication setting, the players can also "deterministically" compute a cut sparsifier and use it to approximate the max-flow/min-cut value with the same complexity.

**Lemma 2.12.** _For any_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)_, there is a deterministic protocol such that Alice and Bob jointly computes an_ \(\varepsilon\)_-cut sparsifier of G with_ \(\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)\) _edges and maximum weight_ \(\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^2n)\)_. The protocol communicates_ \(\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)\) _bits and always succeeds._

**Corollary 2.13.** _For any_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\)_, Alice and Bob can jointly and deterministically compute a value f such that_ \((1-\varepsilon)\nu(G)\le f\le(1+\varepsilon)\nu(G)\) _using_ \(\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)\) _bits of communication._

## 3 Overview

The starting point of our algorithm builds on the work of \[RSW18\]. Their algorithm, in which we will call RSW algorithm, can be viewed as computing a partition of the vertex set whose contraction results in a sparse graph that preserves all _s-t_ minimum cuts. That work focuses exclusively on the cut-query model and yields a randomized algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) query complexity for the task. Upon closer inspection, we observe that the complexity can be parameterized in terms of \(\nu(G)\) depending on the computation models: to \(\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3}\nu(G)^{1/3})\) cut queries and to \(\widetilde{O}(n\cdot\nu(G)^{2/3})\) bits of communication. At first glance, these parameterized improvements may seem unhelpful, as \(\nu(G)\) can be as large as \(\Omega(n)\). However, to state the obvious, when \(\nu(G)\) is truly sublinear, these bounds yield a complexity of \(n^{5/3-\Omega(1)}\) in both models. This observation motivates a simple yet powerful scheme: apply a preprocessing step to _G_ that reduces the _s-t_ min-cut to \(\Delta=o(n)\) while preserving all _s-t_ min-cuts, and then apply the RSW algorithm to the post-processed graph. If this preprocessing can be implemented efficiently, it opens the possibility of achieving overall sub-_n_<sup>5/3</sup> complexity. We summarize this framework in the table below.

**Algorithm 1:** A model-independent framework for computing minimum _s-t_ cuts.

**Input:** An undirected unweighted graph _G_=(_V,E_) with _n_ vertices.

**Output:** A minimum _s-t_ cut of _G_.

**Procedures:**

1. Compute a graph \(H\unknown G\) such that \(\nu(H)\ge\nu(G)-\Delta\) for some value \(\Delta\) to be set later.

1a. Compute a flow subgraph \(F\unknown H\) of value \(\nu(F)=\nu(H)\ge\nu(G)-\Delta\).

2. Compute a minimum _s-t_ cut in the residual network _G<sub>F</sub>_, and output it.

Algorithm 1: A model-independent framework for computing a minimum _s-t_ cut.

Note here that if we assume a correct answer _H_ following Step 1, the flow subgraph _F_ in Step 1a can be computed locally and free of costs in both computation models.

We first need to argue that this is a correct framework. This is done via following claim which gives a perfect reduction between all minimum _s-t_ cuts of _G<sub>F</sub>_ and all minimum _s-t_ cuts of _G_.

**Claim 3.1.** _Let G be an undirected unweighted graph and F be its flow subgraph. For any cut_ (_S,T), we have_ \(|E_G(S,T)|=\nu(F)+w_{G_F}(S,T)\).

_Proof._ First, observe that \(w_{G_F}(S,T)=|E_{G\backslash F}(S,T)|+2\cdot w_F(T,S)\). This is because we can write _G<sub>F</sub>_ as a union of two graphs: an undirected unweighted graph _G_\\_F_ (which contributes to the first term) and a directed graph which is a reversal of edges of _F_ with weights 2 (which contributes to the second term).

Observe further that \(\nu(F)=w_F(S,T)-w_F(T,S)\). This is because the edges of _F_ can be partitioned into \(\nu(F)\) disjoint _s-t_ directed paths. Each of those start at \(s\in S\) and ends at \(t\in T\). As such, it must cross from _S_ to _T_ exactly one more time than it crosses from _T_ to _S_. Thus, each of the \(\nu(F)\) disjoint _s-t_ directed paths contribute a value of 1 to _w<sub>F</sub>(S,T_)-_w<sub>F</sub>(T,S_).

Combining the two observations, we have:

\(\nu(F)+|E_{G_F}(S,T)|=w_F(S,T)+w_F(T,S)+|E_{G\backslash F}(S,T)|=|E_G(S,T)|\)

as wished.

We consider the implementation of Algorithm 1 in two computational models: the _cut-query model_ and the _two-player communication model_, where we aim to use the (modified) RSW algorithm as a baseline to implement Step 2 in both settings. However, applying the RSW algorithm to the residual graph _G<sub>F</sub>_ introduces two key challenges. First, we only have cut-query access to the original graph _G_, not to the residual graph _G<sub>F</sub>_. In fact, throughout our algorithm, we shall only need to make cut queries to the graph _G_\\_F_. Fortunately, since the flow graph _F_ is explicitly computed in Step 1a, we can simulate cut queries to _G_\\_F_ using a single query access to _G_ and the explicit description of _F_. Second, the residual graph _G<sub>F</sub>_ is a _mixed_ graph, containing both directed and undirected edges. As the RSW algorithm was originally designed for undirected graphs, it does not directly apply to this setting. To address this, we show that the RSW algorithm can be carefully modified to operate on mixed graphs in both computational models without altering its correctness.

These modifications also allow for a query and communication complexity to be parameterized by the min-cut/max-flow value of the residual graph _G<sub>F</sub>_ as well.

For now, we summarize the results of applying the modified RSW algorithm in both computational models with the full implementation details deferred to Section 4.

Then, there exists an algorithm that makes_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^{4/3}\nu(\mathcal{G})^{1/3})\) _cut-queries to G and w.h.p. computes a mini mum s-t cut of_ G.

We now restrict our attention to Step 1 as it is key algorithmic design of this work. We first state the results on both computation models.

**Lemma 3.4** (Finding a large flow via cut query)**.** _Let G be an input graph, and let_ \(\Delta\le n\) _be an additive error parameter. Then, there is a randomized algorithm that computes_ \(H\unknown G\) _with_ \(\nu(H)\ge\nu(G)-\Delta\)_. The algorithm makes_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^2}{\sqrt{\Delta}}+\frac{n^3}{\Delta^2}\right)\) _cut queries to G and succeeds w.h.p._

**Lemma 3.5** (Finding a large flow via communication)**.** _Let G be an input graph, and let_ \(\Delta\le n\) _be an additive error parameter. Then, there is a deterministic protocol that computes_ \(H\unknown G\) _with_ \(\nu(H)\ge\nu(G)-\Delta\)_. The protocol uses_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n\cdot\nu(G)}{\sqrt{\Delta}}+\frac{n\cdot\nu(G)^2}{\Delta^2}\right)\) _bits of communication and always succeeds._

Our algorithms for both lemmas share the same principle. To best understand it, we study a simplified question in a model-independent setting: suppose we are given three parameters \(k'<k\le f\) with a promise that \(\nu(G)\ge f\), and also given for free is a graph \(H\unknown G\) such that \(\nu(H)\ge f-k\). Our goal is to sequentially add (a small number of) edges from _G_\\_H_ to _H_ so that it eventually becomes _H_after with \(\nu(H^\mathrm{after})\ge f-k'\). In later sections, we show that an efficient algorithm for this toy question leads to both Lemma 3.4 and Lemma 3.5.

At a high level, our algorithm proceeds in a greedy-like manner. For any graph G, we define a set of _witnesses_, denoted W(G), with an invariant that \(\nu(\mathcal{G})\ge f-k'\) if and only if \(\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{G})=\emptyset\). Our procedure starts with \(H_1\leftarrow H\). In each round _i_=1,2_,..._, we determine an edge \(e_i\in G\backslash H_i\) that reduces the number of witnesses by a non-trivial fraction; that is, _e<sub>i</sub>_ is such that \(|\mathcal{W}(H_i\cup\{e_i\})|\le(1-\gamma)\cdot|\mathcal{W}(H_i)|\) for some fixed value \(\gamma\) that may depend on _n,k_, or \(k'\). We call such edges with that property \(\gamma\)_-good_. We then set \(H_{i+1}\leftarrow H_i\cup\{e_i\}\), and repeat. The procedure terminates at the earliest round _T_ where \(\mathcal{W}(H_T)=\emptyset\), ensuring that the final graph _H_after:=_H<sub>T</sub>_ has \(\nu(H_T)\ge f-k'\) via our invariant.

Following this greedy-like approach, there are two main questions that need to be addressed. First, what is the correct definition of a _witness_? Recall that we want to maintain the invariant that \(\nu(\mathcal{G})\ge f-k'\) if and only if \(\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{G})=\emptyset\). A strong candidate for a witness is a cut of size at most \(f-k'-1\) in G, thanks to the Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem. This, however, is only partially correct. We define a witness as a _redundant_ representation of a small cut on G, consisting of a cut (_S,T_) of small size \(|E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)|\le f-k'-1\), the set _E_<sub>G</sub>(_S,T_) of edges crossing such cut, and a set _X_ of _non-existing edges_ that cross this cut, with \(|X|=f-k'-1-|E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)|\ge 0\). With this notion,<tbc>

we still maintain the invariant, while the added redundancy (i.e., the non-existing edges) allows us to pre-allocate a set of edges that could potentially be added to G in the future, ensuring that the cut value of (_S,T_) remains at most \(f-k'-1\).

**Definition 3.6** (Witness)**.** _Let_ G=(_V,E_) _be an unweighted undirected graph with two designated terminals s and t. A tuple_ W=(_S,T,Y_) _is called a_ witness _of_ G _if the following conditions hold:_

1. (_S,T_) _is an s-t cut of_ G _with value_ \(|E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)|\le f-k'-1\).<tbc>

_2._ \(Y\subseteq S\times T\) _such that_ \(|Y|=f-k'-1\) _and_ \(E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)\subseteq Y\).

_Finally, let_ W(G) _denote the set of all witnesses of_ G.

Notice that the notion of _Y_ here is consistent with \(E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)\cup X\) as explained in the previous paragraph. For clarity, we may relax the notation and write a witness as \((S,T,E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)\cup X)\) if needed. However, it is crucial to view _Y_ as a union of _E_<sub>G</sub>(_S,T_) and _X_ rather than two individual sets _E_<sub>G</sub>(_S,T_) and _X_.

**Invariant 3.7** (Witness Invariant)**.** _For any graph_ G_, we have_ \(\nu(\mathcal{G})\ge f-k'\) _if and only if_ \(\mathcal{W}(\mathcal{G})=\emptyset\).

The second question is how quickly we can decrease the number of witnesses. Following the above definition of witnesses, we can naturally describe how a witness is removed upon an insertion of (_a,b_): say a pair of vertices \((a,b)\notin E\) _ kills_ W iff W is _not_ a witness of \(\mathcal{G}\cup(a,b)\). <sup>5</sup>

Following this description, observe that if \(a\notin S\) or \(b\notin T\), then (_a,b_) can never kill W. Furthermore, even if \(a\in S\) and \(b\in T\) but \((a,b)\in Y\) , then W remains a witness of \(\mathcal{G}\cup(a,b)\). This leads us to the following equivalent interpretation of invalidating a witness.

**Definition 3.8** (Killing a witness)**.** _Let_ G=(_V,E_) _be an unweighted and undirected graph with terminals s and t, and let_ W=(_S,T,Y_) _be one of its witnesses. We say a pair of vertices_ (_a,b_) kills _witness_ W=(_S,T,Y_) _if and only if_ \(a\in S\), \(b\in T\)_, and_ \((a,b)\notin Y\) .

In other words, these conditions together mean that (_a,b_) are on the different side of (_S,T_) and does _not_ belong to the pre-allocated cut _Y_ of (_S,T_), thereby invalidating the witness.

With this definition, we can establish an upper bound _n_<sup>_O(n_)</sup> on the initial number of witnesses. To see this, there are up to 2_<sup>n</sup>_ possible choices of (_S,T_), and for each fixed value of (_S,T_), there are up to \(n^{2(f-k^\prime-1)}\le n^{2n}\) choices of _Y_ . Due to our greedy-like approach, we assert that each iteration reduces the number of witnesses by a fraction of \(\gamma\). Therefore, we only need \(\widetilde{O}(n/\gamma)\) iterations to eliminate all witnesses, thereby terminating the algorithm.

Finally, for this argument to go through, we need to determine an appropriate value of \(\gamma\) such that a \(\gamma\)-good edge always exists in _G_\\_H<sub>i</sub>_ in every iteration _i_. Depending on the computation model, we also need to be able to find such edge efficiently. Without these guarantees, our algorithm may spend too much resource in finding a \(\gamma\)-good edge, or even worse may fail horribly if such edge did not exists at all. This is where the "promise" that \(\nu(G)\ge f\) and the "redundancy" of witness’s definition comes into rescue. Under these assumptions, by setting \(\gamma=\Omega\left(\frac{k'}{n\sqrt{k}}\right)\), a \(\gamma\)-good edge always exists.

<sup>5</sup>Notice that this is defined with respect to a _pair_ of vertices (_a,b_) rather than an _edge_ (_a,b_). This is due to a technical reason that in the cut-query model, we (as an algorithm designer) do not know if (_a,b_) exists in the underlying graph until we somehow "learn" it. For the ease of understanding, it is helpful to think of (_a,b_) as an actual edge in _G_ that is not presented in _H_ yet.

<tbc>**Claim 3.9.** _For any iteration i such that_ \(\mathcal{W}(H_i)\neq\emptyset\)_, there exists an edge_ \(e_i\in G\backslash H_i\) _such that_

\(|\mathcal{W}(H_i\cup e_i)|\le\left(1-\Omega\left(\frac{k'}{n\sqrt{k}}\right)\right)\cdot|\mathcal{W}(H_i)|.\)

For now, we will only sketch the proof of Claim 3.9. Later down the line, we will give a constructive variant of this claim which allows us to efficiently recover such edge _e<sub>i</sub>_ via cut-queries.

_Proof Sketch._ Let \(Q\subseteq G\backslash H_i\) be such that \(|Q|=O(n\sqrt{k})\) and \(\nu(H_i\cup Q)\ge f\). Such set _Q_ exists by construction: take a flow subgraph \(F\unknown H_i\) of size _f-k_ and let _Q_ be the set of all edges in a non-circular flow of size _k_ of _G<sub>F</sub>_ that has not appeared in _H<sub>i</sub>_. The bound of \(|Q|=O(n\sqrt{k})\) is obtained via Lemma 2.2.

Suppose we were to add _Q_ to _H<sub>i</sub>_. For any witness W=(_S,T,Y_) of _H<sub>i</sub>_, there will be at least _f_ edges among \(H_i\cup Q\) that crosses the cut (_S,T_). However, we only pre-allocate \(f-k'-1\) edges to _Y_ and those already include _E<sub>H<sub>i</sub></sub>(S,T_). Thus, there are at least \(k'+1\) edges among _Q_ that kills W. Since this holds for any witness W, via an averaging argument, some edge(s) among _Q_ must kill at least a \(\frac{k'+1}{|Q|}\ge\Omega\left(\frac{k'}{n\sqrt{k}}\right)\) fraction of W(_H<sub>i</sub>_).

**Claim 3.9 is good (enough) for two-player communication.** When edges of _G_ are partitioned across Alice and Bob, each player can locally evaluate, via brute-force, whether each edge is \(\gamma\)-good w.r.t. \(\gamma=\Omega\left(\frac{k'}{n\sqrt{k}}\right)\). Claim 3.9 guarantees that such good edge always exists among _G_\\_H_; thus must be found by one of the players. Such player then spends \(\widetilde{O}(1)\) bits of communication to send over that edge, adds it to _H_, and then proceeds to the next iteration. As a result, the total communication cost is \(\widetilde{O}(n/\gamma)=\widetilde{O}(n^2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{k'})\). Then, following a line of reduction, we can recover a weaker version of Lemma 3.5 with communication cost replaced by \(\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^2}{\sqrt{\Delta}}+\frac{n^3}{\Delta^2}\right)\). For all intents and purposes, we can use this weaker result to recover an \(\widetilde{O}(n^{11/7})\) communication protocol by combining it with Lemma 3.3. However, to get a parameterized complexity of \(\widetilde{O}(n\cdot\nu(G)^{4/7})\) as promised in Lemma 3.5, we need to strengthen our strategy. We defer this improvement to Section C.

**It is a bit more complicated for cut-query.** In the communication model, our search for a \(\gamma\)-good edge leverages a crucial feature: the input graph is _explicitly_ given, although being split between players. This guarantees that any \(\gamma\)-good edge must already be visible to at least one of them. In contrast, the cut-query model lacks this advantage, as we can only make queries to a _hidden_ graph. Given the somewhat-artificial definition of a \(\gamma\)-good edge, it is not immediately clear whether such an edge can be efficiently identified. Fortunately, we develop an alternative proof of Claim 3.9 that is constructive! This new approach--combined with a few additional subroutines--allows us to locate an \(\Omega(\gamma)\)-good edge (with a slightly worse constant factor) using only _O_(log_n_) cut queries to _G_. We explore this approach in detail in Section 5.

We begin by studying a useful combinatorial structure: a _forest packing_. Let _G_ be an undirected, unweighted graph. For any integer \(k\ge 1\), we define a _k-forest packing_ of _G_ to be \(P=F_1\cup\dots\cup F_k\) where, for each \(i\in[k]\), the subgraph _F<sub>i</sub>_ is a spanning forest of the graph \(G\backslash(F_1\cup\dots\cup F_{i-1})\). A crucial insight is that any _k_-forest packing yields a relatively sparse subgraph of _G_ that simultaneously preserves all small cuts and ensures that large cuts remain large. These properties are formally captured in the following lemma.

**Lemma 4.2.** _Let P be k-forest packing of a graph G. Then, the following statements are true._

1. _For a cut_ (_S,T), if_ \(|E_G(S,T)|\le k\)_, then E<sub>P</sub>(S,T_)=_E<sub>G</sub>(S,T)._<tbc>

_2._ _For a cut_ (_S,T), if_ \(|E_G(S,T)|\ge k+1\)_, then_ \(|E_P(S,T)|\ge k\).<tbc>

_3._ _P has average degree O(k)._

If there is an edge among _E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_) remained in \(G\backslash(F_1\cup\dots\cup F_{i-1})\), the spanning forest _F<sub>i</sub>_ must include at least one of those remaining edges. In other words, upon packing \(k\ge|E_G(S,T)|\) spanning forest into _P_, all edges of _E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_) must be included. This means _E<sub>P</sub>(S,T_)=_E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_).

For (2), we have two cases. First, if \(E_{F_i}(S,T)=\emptyset\) for some \(i\in[k]\), it means all edges in _E<sub>G</sub>(S,T_) must have already been included in \(F_1\cup\dots\cup F_{i-1}\). In this case, we can write \(|E_P(S,T)|=\sum_{i\in[k]}|E_{F_i}(S,T)|\ge k\) as wished.

Finally, we prove (3). Notice that each _F<sub>i</sub>_ has at most _n_-1 edges. Thus, the number of edges in _P_ is at most _k(n_-1), implying that the average degree is at most \(\frac{2k(n-1)}{n}=O(k)\).

\(Pr_{(Z,Y)\sim(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{Y})}\left[(u,v)\text{\textit{kills}}(Z,Y)\right]\ge\frac{k'+1}{k}\cdot|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|.\)

_Proof._ Recall that, by definition, an edge (_u,v_) _kills_ a witness (_S,T,Y_) if \(z_u\neq z_v\)--i.e., _u_ and _v_ lie on opposite sides of the cut--and \((u,v)\notin Y\) . Under this characterization, the LHS quantity becomes: \(Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{Z}}(z_u\neq z_v)\cdot Pr_{(Z,Y)\sim(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{Y}|z_u\neq z_v)}\left[(u,v)\text{kills}(Z,Y)|z_u\neq z_v\right].\) By Claim 5.3, we have \(Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{Z}}(z_u\neq z_v)\ge|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\). Moreover, we can bound the second term by: \(Pr_{(Z,Y)\sim(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{Y}|z_u\neq z_v)}\left[(u,v)\text{kills}(Z,Y)|z_u\neq z_v\right]\)
\(=\sum_{Z\in supp(\mathcal{Z}|z_u\neq z_v)}Pr\left(\mathcal{Z}=Z|z_u\neq z_v\right)\cdot Pr_{Y\sim\mathcal{Y}|Z}\left[(u,v)\notin Y\backslash E_H(S,T)|Z\right])\)
\(\ge\sum_{Z\in supp(\mathcal{Z}|z_u\neq z_v)}Pr\left(\mathcal{Z}=Z|z_u\neq z_v\right)\cdot\frac{k'+1}{k}\) (Claim 5.4) \(=\frac{k'+1}{k}\cdot\sum_{Z\in supp(\mathcal{Z}|z_u\neq z_v)}Pr\left(\mathcal{Z}=Z|z_u\neq z_v\right)\)
\(=\frac{k'+1}{k}.\) Multiplying the two bounds completes the proof. We emphasize that Claim 5.5 is vastly useful in our analysis, as it applies to every edge \((u,v)\in G\backslash H\). Recall that the distribution (Z,Y) is a uniform among all remaining witnesses. Hence, the claim then implies that any edge \((u,v)\in G\backslash H\) kills an \(\Omega\left(|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\right)\) fraction of the current witnesses. Furthermore, given the current subgraph _H_, the values \(\hat{z}_v\) for all \(v\in V\) can be computed locally with no extra costs. As a result, our task is significantly simplified: it suffices to identify an edge \((u,v)\in G\backslash H\) such that \(|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\ge\gamma\) for some suitable threshold \(\gamma>0\). The following claim ensures the existence of such an edge, with \(\gamma=\Omega\left(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\right)\). **Claim 5.6.** _There exists an edge_ \((u,v)\in G\backslash H\) _such that_ \(|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\ge\alpha\cdot\frac{k'}{n\sqrt{k}}\)_, for some universal constant_ \(\alpha>0\). _Proof._ For any support \(Z\in supp(\mathcal{Z})\) (meaning that _Z_=(_S,T_) appears in some witness), we have \(\sum_{(u,v)\in H}|z_u-z_v|\le f-k'-1\) following the equivalent definition of witness in (3). Taking expectation over _Z_∼Z, we have: \(f-k'-1\ge\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{Z}}\sum_{(u,v)\in H}|z_u-z_v|\)
\(=\sum_{(u,v)\in H}\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{Z}}|z_u-z_v|\) (linearity of expectation)
\(\ge\sum_{(u,v)\in H}\left|\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{Z}}z_u-\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{Z}}z_v\right|\) (triangle inequality)
\(=\sum_{(u,v)\in H}|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|.\) On the other hand, let \(Q\subseteq G\backslash H\) be such that \(|Q|=O(n\sqrt{k})\) and \(\nu(H\cup Q)=f\). The existence of _Q_ is guaranteed via construction. Let \(F\unknown H\) be a flow subgraph of _H_ with \(\nu(F)=\nu(H)\ge f-k\).

We then have \(\nu(G_F)=\nu(G)-\nu(F)\ge f-\nu(F)\). We then let \(F'\) be a non-circular flow of _GF_ with value \(f-\nu(F)\) and set \(Q=F'\backslash H\). We then see that \(\nu(H\cup Q)\ge\nu(F')+\nu(F)=f\) and \(|Q|\le|F'|\le O(n\sqrt{f-\nu(F)})\le O(n\sqrt{k})\) due to Lemma 2.2. As a result, we derive: \(\sum_{(u,v)\in H\cup Q}|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\ge\sum_{i\in[f]}\sum_{\left(u,v\right)\text{in}i^\text{th}s\text{-}t\text{flow}}|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\)
\(\ge\sum_{i\in[f]}|\hat{z}_t-\hat{z}_s|\) (triangle inequality)
\(=f(\hat{z}_s=0\text{and}\hat{z}_t=1.)\) This implies \(\sum_{(u,v)\in Q}|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\ge k'+1\) which means some edge \((u,v)\in Q\subseteq G\backslash H\) must have \(|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\ge\frac{k'+1}{|Q|}\ge\Omega\left(\frac{k'}{n\sqrt{k}}\right)\). By combining Claim 5.5 and Claim 5.6, there must exist of an edge \((u,v)\in G\backslash H\) that kills a \(\frac{k'+1}{k}\cdot\left(\alpha\cdot\frac{k'}{n\sqrt{k}}\right)\approx\frac{\alpha}{4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\) fraction of the remaining witnesses, via the fact that \(k'=\frac{k}{2}\). In the next section, we introduce a subroutine that, using only _O_(log_n_) cut queries, enables us to find an edge in _G_\\_H_ that is (asymptotically) as effective as such edge (_u,v_). ## 5.3 Useful Subroutines Consider the following problem called `FindLongEdge`. We are given the following items as an input. • An underlying graph _G_=(_V,E_) to which we are able to make cut-query. • A potential function \(\phi:V\rightarrow[0,1]\) that maps \(v\in V\) to its position between 0 and 1. • A threshold \(\delta\in(0,1)\). There is also a hidden parameter \(\delta_\mathrm{max}:=\mathrm{max}_{(u,v)\in E}|\phi(u)-\phi(v)|\) not known to us. We are asked to identify a _long_ edge--if one exists--whose endpoints are mapped far apart, by making cut queries to _G_. Formally, we must output either • \((u,v)\in G\) with \(|\phi(u)-\phi(v)|\ge\frac{\delta}{2}\), or • "FAIL" which means \(\delta>\delta_\mathrm{max}\). Another helpful interpretation is as follows. If \(\delta\le\delta_\mathrm{max}\), then we must output \((u,v)\in G\) with \(|\phi(u)-\phi(v)|\ge\delta/2\). On the other hand, if \(\delta>\delta_\mathrm{max}\), it is acceptable to output either such (_u,v_), if existed, or "FAIL". We first describe a useful object that will shortly help us design an algorithm for `FindLongEdge`. Let \(\ell\) be an arbitrary positive integer. We call \(A=((p_1,q_1),\dots,(p_\ell,q_\ell))\) an _assignment_ iff for each _i_ we have \((p_i,q_i)\in\{1,2,3\}\times\{1,2\}\) and \(p_i\neq p_{i+1}\). We say a pair \((i,j)\in[\ell]^2\) is _matched_ by _A_ iff _pi=pj_ and \(q_i\neq q_j\). By the description of assignments, we notice that any pairs (_i,j_) with \(|i-j|\le 1\) is never matched. The following claim shows that all remaining pairs can be matched at least once if we are allowed to have \(O(\mathrm{log}\ell)\) assignments. **Claim 5.7.** _There exists a set of_ \(t=O(\mathrm{log}\ell)\) _assignments_ A={_A_(1)_,...,A_(_t_)} _such that every pair_ \((i,j)\in[\ell]^2\) _with_ \(|i-j|\ge 2\) _is matched by at least one assignment among_ A.

_Proof._ We will prove the existence via a probabilistic argument. Consider the following random process for constructing an assignment \(A=\left((p_1,q_1),\dots,(p_\ell,q_\ell)\right)\). 1. Assign _p_1=1. 2. For any \(2\le i\le\ell\), sequentially assign _pi_ uniformly at random among {1,2,3}\\{_p__i_-1} 3. For each _j_, assign \(q_j\in\{1,2\}\) independently. We make the following miniclaim: for any (_i,j_) that \(|i-j|\ge 2\), we have (_i,j_) being matched by _A_ with probability at least \(\frac{1}{8}\). To see this, assume WLOG that \(i\ge j+2\). Then, we have \(\mathrm{Pr}(p_i=p_j)=\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-1}=p_j)\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(p_i=p_j|p_{i-1}=p_j)+\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-1}\neq p_j)\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(p_i=p_j|p_{i-1}\neq p_j)\)
\(=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-1}\neq p_j)\) since Pr(_pi=pj|p__i_-1=_pj_)=0 and \(\mathrm{Pr}(p_i=p_j|p_{i-1}\neq p_j)=\frac{1}{2}\). Moreover, we have \(\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-1}\neq p_j)\)
\(=\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-2}=p_j)\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-1}\neq p_j|p_{i-2}=p_j)+\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-2}\neq p_j)\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-1}\neq p_j|p_{i-1}\neq p_j)\)
\(=\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-2}=p_j)+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-2}\neq p_j)\)
\(=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-2}=p_j).\) where the second equality is true via the construction: we have \(\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-1}\neq p_j|p_{i-2}=p_j)=1\) and \(\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-1}\neq p_j|p_{i-1}\neq p_j)=\frac{1}{2}\). It is worth noting that these chain of equations subtly relies on the assumption that \(i\ge j+2\). This condition ensures that our random process assigns a value to _pj,...,p__i_-2_,p__i_-1, and _pi_ in that particular order. Combining the two equations, we have \(\mathrm{Pr}(p_i=p_j)=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(p_{i-2}=p_j)\ge\frac{1}{4}\). Since _qi_ and _qj_ are assigned uniformly and independently among {1,2}, and independent of _pi_ and _pj_, we have \(\mathrm{Pr}(p_i=p_j\wedge q_i\neq q_j)=\mathrm{Pr}(p_i=p_j)\cdot\mathrm{Pr}(q_i\neq q_j)\ge\frac{1}{8}.\) In other words, (_i,j_) are matched by _A_ with probability at least \(\frac{1}{8}\), thereby proving our miniclaim. Now consider drawing _t_=24log_n_ independently random assignments from the above process. As a consequence, there must be a deterministic choice of those _t_ assignments that the statement remains true, thereby proving our claim. (1) For each assignment \(A=((p_1,q_1),\dots,(p_\ell,q_\ell))\in\mathcal{A}\), we do:<tbc>

(1a) Partition _V_ into 6 sets. Namely, for each \((r,s)\in\{1,2,3\}\times\{1,2\}\), we denote:<tbc>

<tbc>\(V_{r,s}:=\{v\in V|\phi(v)\in I_j\wedge(r,s)=(p_j,q_j)\}.\)<tbc>

We now justify the correctness of our algorithm, which follows from these two miniclaims.

1. If \(\delta\le\delta_\mathrm{max}\), then the algorithm never outputs "FAIL", i.e. it must output some edge (_u,v_).<tbc>

2. If the algorithm outputs some edge (_u,v_), then we have \(|\phi(u)-\phi(v)|\ge\frac{\delta}{2}\) .<tbc>

### 5.4 Putting All Together: Proof of Claim 5.1

We now combine all the pieces to prove our main claim of this section.

**Claim 5.1.** _Let f,k be known parameters with a promise that_ \(\nu(G)\ge f\)_, and also given explicitly is a subgraph_ \(H\unknown G\) _with_ \(\nu(H)\ge f-k\)_. Set_ \(k'=\frac{k}{2}\)_. Then, there is a deterministic algorithm which makes_ \(\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^2}{\sqrt{k}}\right)\) _cut queries to G and outputs_ \(H^\mathrm{after}\unknown G\) _with_ \(\nu(H^\mathrm{after})\ge f-k'=f-\frac{k}{2}\).

_Proof._ We do as follows.

1. If \(\mathcal{W}(H)=\emptyset\), output the current _H_ and terminate. Otherwise, proceed.<tbc>

2. Compute \(\hat{z}_v\) for all \(v\in V\) w.r.t. _H_.<tbc>

3. Use the algorithm of Lemma 5.8 to compute `FindLongEdge` with respect to the graph _G_\\_H_, potential \(\phi(v):=\hat{z}_v\) and \(\delta:=\frac{\alpha}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\). Let \((u,v)\in G\backslash H\) be the edge that is outputted.<tbc>

4. Set \(H\leftarrow H\cup(u,v)\) and go back to Step 1.

If our algorithm ever terminates, its correctness follows from Invariant 3.7 that \(\mathcal{W}(H)=\emptyset\) implies \(\nu(H)\ge f-k'\). Thus, it suffice to justify the termination and query complexity.

Assume that at the start of an iteration, we have \(\mathcal{W}(H)\neq\emptyset\). Claim 5.6 tells us that some \((u^*,v^*)\in G\backslash H\) has \(|\hat{z}_{u^*}-\hat{z}_{v^*}|\ge\frac{\alpha}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\) ; i.e. the graph _G_\\_H_ has \(\delta_\mathrm{max}\ge\frac{\alpha}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}=\delta\). This means Step 2 successfully finds \((u,v)\in G\backslash H\) such that \(|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\ge\frac{\delta}{2}=\frac{\alpha}{4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\) per the guarantee of Lemma 5.8. Thus, via Claim 5.5, the fraction of W(_H_) that (_u,v_) kills is at least \(\frac{k'+1}{k}\cdot|\hat{z}_u-\hat{z}_v|\ge\frac{\alpha}{8}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\) . As a result, upon inserting (_u,v_) to _H_, the number of remaining witnesses is reduced to

\(\mathcal{W}(H\cup(u,v))\le\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{8}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\right)\cdot\mathcal{W}(H)\le\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{\alpha}{8}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k}}{n}\right)\cdot\mathcal{W}(H).\)

A trivial bound shows that in the beginning, we have at most _n_<sup>_O(n_)</sup> witnesses. Therefore, we only need

\(\left(\frac{8}{\alpha}\cdot\frac{n}{\sqrt{k}}\right)\cdot\mathrm{log}\left(n^{O(n)}\right)=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^2}{\sqrt{k}}\right)\)

iterations before all witnesses are killed. Then, in the next iteration, the algorithm will surely terminate.

Finally, we need to bound the number of cut queries made to _G_. Consider an arbitrary iteration which _H_ has been given explicitly. Only Line 3 requires us to make _O_(log_n_) cut queries to _G_\\_H_. Each of which can be simulated by a single query to _G_, along with an explicit description of _H_. Since the algorithm only needs \(\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^2}{\sqrt{k}}\right)\) iterations, we only make \(\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^2}{\sqrt{k}}\right)\) cut queries to _G_.

## 6 Open Problems

We conclude with a brief discussion of open problems and future directions motivated by our results.

## SFM Lower Bounds via Graph Cuts.

The current best deterministic lower bound for submodular function minimization (SFM) is due to Chakrabarty, Graur, Jiang, and Sidford \[CGJS22\], who showed that any algorithm must make at least \(\Omega(nlogn)\) value queries to solve SFM in the value oracle model. Their construction involves a carefully designed submodular function tailored to their lower bound framework. This raises the intriguing open question of whether any variants of graph cut functions can be used to establish a matching \(\Omega(nlogn)\) lower bound. In particular, obtaining an \(\Omega(n^{1.01})\) lower bound for SFM, whether via graph cuts or not, would be considered a major breakthrough.

## SFM Upper Bound and Directed/Weighted Graphs.

On the upper bound side of SFM, the best-known algorithm by Jiang \[Jia23\] makes \(\widetilde{O}(n^2)\) value queries. An obvious major open problem is to achieve, e.g., \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\) bound for some constant \(\epsilon>0\). Towards this goal, computing the minimum _s-t_ cuts on directed/weighted graphs presents a major barrier as _no o(n_<sup>2</sup>) algorithm was known for _either_ the case of directed unweighted graphs and case of undirected weighted graphs (despite many progress in the sequential and other settings \[BGJV25; BCK+24; BCP+23; CKL+22; BGJ+22; BLL+21; BLN+20\]). We believe that presenting an \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\) bound for one of these cases will be a major progress. In particular, for the directed case, even a more apparent barrier is to solving the following simple _reachability_ problem \[Nan24\]: Can we determine if there is a _directed s-t_ path in an unweighted directed graph in \(O(n^{2-\epsilon})\) cut queries for some constant \(\epsilon>0\)? It should be a breakthrough already to solve this reachability problem.

For the _global_ min-cut problem, the cut query complexity is essentially resolved for weighted undirected graphs \[MN20\]. While there has been progress in the standard sequential setting \[CLN+21\], we are not aware of any new developments in the cut query model. We leave this as another important open problem.

## Finding a Maximum Flow.

The duality between the minimum _s-t_ cut and the maximum _s-t_ flow is one of the most celebrated results in combinatorial optimization. While our algorithm computes (and enumerates all) minimum _s-t_ cuts, it does not immediately yield a maximum _s-t_ flow. This limitation is also shared by the algorithm of Rubinstein, Schramm, and Weinberg \[RSW18\]. On the other hand, the deterministic algorithm of Anand, Saranurak, and Wang \[ASW25\] does output a maximum _s-t_ flow using \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) cut queries and communication. Interestingly, a closer examination of our approach reveals that it too can be extended to recover a maximum flow with complexity \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\): by applying either Lemma 3.4 or Lemma 3.5 with threshold \(\Delta=n^{2/3}\), and then augmenting to a full maximum flow using _O(n_<sup>2/3</sup>) additional iterations of the standard augmenting path method. Nevertheless, it remains an intriguing open problem whether one can compute a maximum _s-t_ flow using fewer than _o(n_<sup>5/3</sup>) cut queries or bits of communication. Doing so with _combinatorial algorithms_, even for the special case of bipartite matching \[BBE+22\] will also be interesting.

## Improving Query Complexity.

Our \(\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})\)-query algorithm (Theorem 1.1) represents the first progress beyond the \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) barrier established by \[RSW18\] and \[ASW25\], demonstrating that this bound is not optimal. A natural next milestone is to design an algorithm with complexity \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})\). Although the support size of a minimum _s-t_ cut is at most _O(n_), it is reasonable to conjecture a lower bound of \(\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{3/2})\) for the problem, as this matches the support size of its dual--the maximum _s-t_ flow of value \(\Omega(n)\). In fact, one can show that any algorithm which outputs an exact maximum flow--or even a multiplicative \(\Omega(1)\)-approximation--must incur a communication complexity of \(\Omega(n^{3/2})\) bits, and therefore a cut-query complexity of \(\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{3/2})\). From the lower bound perspective,<tbc>

<tbc>showing that any deterministic two-player communication protocol for exactly computing the _value_ of the minimum _s-t_ cut requires \(\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{3/2})\) bits of communication would be an exciting result.

### Improving Combinatorial Protocols.

Similarly, it is natural to ask whether a \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})\)-bit protocol for computing minimum _s-t_ cuts can be achieved using combinatorial techniques. The work of \[GJ25\] confirms that such an upper bound is indeed possible, but their protocol relies on non-combinatorial continuous optimization approaches. We leave it as an open question whether this \(\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})\) bound can be matched by a fully combinatorial protocol. Our \(\widetilde{O}(n^{11/7})\)-bit deterministic protocol (Theorem 1.2) represents progress in this direction.

### Deterministic Algorithms.

While our \(\widetilde{O}(n^{11/7})\) protocol for the two-party communication model is fully deterministic, our \(\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})\) cut-query algorithm is randomized. To date, the only known deterministic cut-query algorithm for computing a minimum _s-t_ cut is the \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\)-query algorithm of \[ASW25\], which is based on a careful implementation of Dinitz’s blocking flow method. It remains an open question whether this \(\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})\) bound can be improved in the deterministic setting.

Notably, our \(\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})\) algorithm is deterministic except for one component: the computation of an \(\varepsilon\)-cut sparsifier. Hence, a deterministic algorithm for constructing such a sparsifier using \(\widetilde{O}(n/\varepsilon^2)\) cut queries would immediately yield a fully deterministic \(\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})\)-query algorithm for the minimum _s-t_ cut problem under our framework. Moreover, via the reduction of \[ASW25\], such an improvement would also extend to computing global minimum cuts deterministically within the same query complexity, up to polylogarithmic factors.

### All-Pairs Min-Cut.

Another natural problem in the cut-query model is to compute the _all- pairs_ min-cut of a graph. Simultaneous to our work, Kenneth-Mordoch and Krauthgamer \[KK25a\] presented the first non-trivial algorithm for this problem, requiring \(\widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})\) randomized cut queries. Given the recent progress in the sequential setting, where the complexity of all-pairs min-cut has been nearly matched to that of an _s-t_ min-cut \[ALPS23; AKL+25; GKYY25\], it is natural to ask whether a similar equivalence can be achieved in the cut-query model. A weaker, yet still interesting, open question is whether one can improve upon the complexity of \(\widetilde{O}(n^{7/4})\) in either the cut-query or two-player communication setting, which is already an interesting problem in its own right.

**Lemma 2.2.** _Let F_=(_V,E_) _be a non-circular flow graph of value f with n vertices. Then, F contains_ \(|E|\le O(n\sqrt{f})\) _edges._

_Proof._ Since _F_ contains no cycles, there exists an topological ordering \(\phi:V\rightarrow[n]\) such that for any directed edge \((a,b)\in E\), we have \(\phi(a)<\phi(b)\). For any edge \(e=(a,b)\in E\), denote \(\phi(e)=\phi(b)-\phi(a)\). We shall also write _e_ and (_a,b_) interchangeably.

We will compute \(X=\sum_{e\in E}w_F(e)\cdot\phi(e)\) in two different ways:

1. Let the _f_ units of flow of _F_ be F<sub>1</sub>_,...,_F_<sub>f</sub>_ where each flow is a (disjoint) directed path from _s_ to _t_. Consider any flow F_<sub>i</sub>_=(_s=v_<sub>0</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>d</sub>=t_). Then, we have:

\(\sum_{e\in\mathcal{F}_i}\phi(e)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\phi(v_{j+1})-\phi(v_j)=\phi(v_d)-\phi(v_0)\le n.\)

Since \(F=\bigcup_{i=1}^f\mathcal{F}_i\), we can compute _X_ by summing over the flows: \(X=\sum_{e\in E}w_F(e)\cdot\phi(e)=\sum_{i=1}^f\sum_{e\in\mathcal{F}_i}\phi(e)\le\sum_{i=1}^fn=nf.\) \(\text{(4)}\) 2. For any vertex \(v\in V\) , let _N(v_) denote the set of out-neighbors of _v_. Then, we can compute _X_ by summing over the vertices: \(X=\sum_{e\in E}w_F(e)\cdot\phi(e)=\sum_{v\in V}\sum_{u\in N(v)}w_F(v,u)\cdot\phi(v,u)\)
\(\ge\sum_{v\in V}\sum_{u\in N(v)}\phi(v,u)\text{(weights are at least 1)}\)
\(=\sum_{v\in V}\sum_{u\in N(v)}(\phi(u)-\phi(v)).\) Since \(\phi\) is an injection and is a topological ordering, the values \(\phi(u)-\phi(v)\) among \(u\in N(v)\) are all distinct positive integers. Therefore, we have: \(\sum_{u\in N(v)}(\phi(u)-\phi(v))\ge\sum_{j=1}^{|N(v)|}j\ge\frac{1}{2}\cdot|N(v)|^2.\) Continuing the bound for _X_, we get: \(X\ge\sum_{v\in V}\frac{1}{2}\cdot|N(v)|^2\ge\frac{1}{2n}\cdot|E|^2\) \(\text{(5)}\) where the last inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz and the fact that \(|E|=\sum_{v\in V}|N(v)|\). Such graph must exist due to Theorem 2.6, thereby must be found by Alice. Bob then does the same to compute _HB_ w.r.t. his graph _GB_. The player then exchange _HA_ and _HB_, and output \(H_A\cup H_B\) as an \(\varepsilon\)-cut sparsifier of \(G=G_A\cup G_B\). \(\le(1+\varepsilon)\cdot|E_{G_A}(S,T)|+(1+\varepsilon)\cdot|E_{G_B}(S,T)|\)

## B Spectral Sparsification with Optimal Weights

For any undirected graph _G_=(_V,E_) with a nonnegative weight function _w<sub>G</sub>_, denote its _Laplacian matrix_ by

\(L_G:=\sum_{e\in E}w_G(e)\cdot\chi_e\chi_e^\top\)

whereas \(\chi_e=e_a-e_b\) for an edge _e_=(_a,b_).

We say a graph _H_ is an \(\varepsilon\)_-spectral sparsifier_ of _G_ iff \(E(H)\subseteq E(G)\) and for any \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), we have

\(1-\varepsilon\le\frac{v^\top L_Hv}{v^\top L_Gv}\le 1+\varepsilon.\)

As a corner case, we note that any Laplacian of a connected graph has null space spanned by an all-one vector \(\vec{1}\). Therefore, it suffices to consider only vectors _v_ that are orthogonal to \(\vec{1}\).

**Observation B.1.** _An_ \(\varepsilon\)_-spectral sparsifier is also an_ \(\varepsilon\)_-cut sparsifier._

The goal of this section is to show that any unweighted undirected graph _G_ has an \(\varepsilon\)-spectral sparsifer with an optimal tradeoff between the number of edges and the maximum weights, as stated in Theorem 2.6. We begin by introducing necessary tools, and then proceed to prove the theorem.

### B.1 Preliminaries

For any matrix \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), denote \(\lambda_1(M)\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n(M)\) to be its eigenvalues in a decreasing order. We say a matrix _M_ is _positive semidefinite_ (or _psd_ for short) iff \(\lambda_n(M)\ge 0\).

For any connected graph _G_=(_V,E_), its Laplacian _L<sub>G</sub>_ is symmetric and is psd. Plus, _L<sub>G</sub>_ has _n_-1 non-zero eigenvalues, and its kernel is of dimension 1 and spanned by \(\vec{1}\). Hence, we can write

\(L_G:=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_iu_iu_i^\top\)

where \(\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_{n-1}>0\) are the top _n_-1 eigenvalues of _L<sub>G</sub>_ and _u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u_<sub>_n_-1</sub> are the corresponding orthonormal eigenvectors. Note that its bottom eigenvalue is \(\lambda_n=0\) with respect to an orthonormal eigenvector is \(u_n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\cdot\vec{1}\).

Denote a Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of _L<sub>G</sub>_ as:<tbc>

\(L_G^+=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\lambda_i}u_iu_i^\top\)

<tbc>and its "square root" as<tbc>

\(L_G^{+/2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_i}}u_iu_i^\top.\)

<tbc>Also denote

\(\Pi=L_G^{+/2}L_GL_G^{+/2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}u_iu_i^\top\)

to be a projection matrix on to the range of _L<sub>G</sub>_.

**Observation B.2.** _The matrices_ \(L_G,L_G^+,L_G^{+/2}\)_, and_ \(\Pi\) _have the same set of orthogonal eigenvectors u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u_<sub>_n_-1</sub> _and_ \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\cdot\vec{1}\)_. They also share the same kernel which is_ \(span(\vec{1})\).

For any edge _e_, denote \(R_e:=\chi_e^\top L_G^+\chi_e\). This quantity is also known as _effective resistance_. A trace argument asserts that the weighted effective resistances sums up to exactly _n_-1. This is known as the Forster’s Theorem.

**Theorem B.3.** _For a connected graph G, we have_ \(\sum_{e\in G}w_eR_e=n-1\).

The following theorem characterizes the top and bottom eigenvalue of a matrix.

**Theorem B.4** (Courant-Fischer formula)**.** \(\lambda_1(M)=max_{v\neq\vec{0}}\frac{v^\top Mv}{v^\top v}\) _and_ \(\lambda_n(M)=min_{v\neq\vec{0}}\frac{v^\top Mv}{v^\top v}\) .

**Corollary B.5.** _For any vector_ \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\)_, an_ \(n\times n\) _matrix_ \(vv^\top\) _is psd. Moreover, we have_ \(\lambda_1(vv^\top)=\|v\|_2^2\).

_Proof._ For any \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), we have \(x^\top(vv^\top)x=\|x^\top v\|_2^2\ge 0\). Thus, \(vv^\top\) is psd. Furthermore, for \(x\neq 0^n\), we have

\(\frac{x^\top(vv^\top)x}{\|x\|_2^2}=\frac{\|x^\top v\|_2^2}{\|x\|_2^2}=\frac{\langle x,v\rangle^2}{\|x\|_2^2}\le\|v\|^2\)

due to the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality. Moreover, the equality is attained when _x=v_. This implies \(\lambda_1(vv^\top)=\|v\|_2^2\) as wished.

We will later need the following matrix concentration bounds which is a simple extension of the the matrix Chernoff bounds \[Tro11\].

**Theorem B.6** (Extended Matrix Chernoff Bounds)**.** _Consider a finite sequence_ {_X<sub>k</sub>_} _of independent random, psd symmetric matrices of dimension n. Let R be a positive scalar such that each of the random matrix satisfies_ \(\lambda_1(X_k)\le R\) _almost surely. Also let_ \(\{\widetilde{X}_l\}\) _be a finite of (deterministic) symmetric psd matrices. Denote_ \(\mathsf{X}=\sum_{i\in[k]}X_i+\sum_{j\in[l]}\widetilde{X}_j\)_. Finally, define:_<tbc>

\(\mu_\mathrm{min}:=\lambda_n(\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{X}])\text{\textit{and}}\mu_\mathrm{max}:=\lambda_1(\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{X}]).\)

<tbc>_Then for any_ \(\delta\in(0,1)\)_, we have:_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Pr}\left[\lambda_1(\mathsf{X})\ge(1+\delta)\mu_\mathrm{max}\right]\le n\cdot\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{\delta^2\mu_\mathrm{max}}{3R}\right)\)

<tbc>_and_

\(\mathrm{Pr}\left[\lambda_n(\mathsf{X})\le(1-\delta)\mu_\mathrm{min}\right]\le n\cdot\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{\delta^2\mu_\mathrm{min}}{2R}\right).\)

We make a few remarks regarding the theorem. First of all, unlike the original statement of \[Tro11\], here we include a set of deterministic matrices \(\{\widetilde{X}_l\}\). Secondly, we will eventually apply such theorem with a set of matrices that yields \(\mathbb{E}[\mathsf{X}]=\Pi\) whose eigenvalues are 1 with multiplicity _n_-1 and 0 with multiplicity 1 (w.r.t. eigenvector \(\vec{1}\)). Since it suffices to only work with vectors orthogonal to \(\vec{1}\), we can treat \(\Pi\) as having all eigenvalues 1.<sup>9</sup> These assumptions we made do not affect the integrity of such theorem nor of our proofs.

<sup>9</sup>To see this, let \(\Pi':=\Pi+\frac{1}{n}\cdot\vec{1}\vec{1}^\top\) so that it has the same set of eigenvectors as \(\Pi\) but now all eigenvalues are 1s. Then, for any vector \(v\perp\vec{1}\), we have \(v^\top\Pi'v=v^\top\Pi v\).

## C.1 Pre-processing _H_

As an initial step, we apply a pre-processing procedure to _H_ as follows:

1. Alice computes a spanning forest F_<sub>A</sub>_ of her full input graph _G<sub>A</sub>_=(_V,E<sub>A</sub>_). She then sends F_<sub>A</sub>_ to Bob and adds it to _H_.<tbc>

2. Bob computes a spanning forest F_<sub>B</sub>_ of his full input graph _G<sub>B</sub>_=(_V,E<sub>B</sub>_). He then sends F_<sub>B</sub>_ to Alice and adds it to _H_.<tbc>

3. The players then combine \(\mathcal{F}_A\cup\mathcal{F}_B\) and compute a set of vertices \(V'\subseteq V\) , consisting of vertices in _V_ that are reachable from _s_ via \(\mathcal{F}_A\cup\mathcal{F}_B\).<tbc>

4. Alice and Bob remove all vertices in \(V\backslash V'\) from their respective private graphs and from the public graph _H_.

This pre-processing procedure is relatively cheap in communication: it requires only 2 rounds of communication and incurs a cost of \(\widetilde{O}(n)\) bits. A key observation is that the graph \(\mathcal{F}_A\cup\mathcal{F}_B\) preserves pairwise connectivity of vertices in _G_. That is, a pair of vertices _u_ and _v_ is connected in _G_ if and only if they are connected in \(\mathcal{F}_A\cup\mathcal{F}_B\). Therefore, the vertex set \(V'\) obtained in Step 3 represents all the vertices in _V_ that are reachable from _s_ in _G_.

The consequences of this pre-processing are as follows. Steps 1 and 2 only add edges to _H_, ensuring that \(\nu(H)\) never decreases. The deletions in Step 4 do not affect the max-flow value of either _G_ or _H_, because any vertex not reachable from _s_ cannot participate in any _s-t_ flow. Thus, the pre-conditions of Claim C.1 remain valid after the pre-processing.

Moreover, after the pre-processing, the vertex set of _H_ becomes \(V'\), and _H_ contains \(\mathcal{F}_A\cup\mathcal{F}_B\) as a subgraph. Consequently, every vertex in _H_ is reachable from _s_, enabling us to assert the following assumption.

**Assumption C.3.** _In the public graph H, every vertex_ \(v\in V(H)\) _is reachable from s._

## C.2 Residual Witness

We now formally define the revised notion of witness in which we call a _residual witness_.

**Definition C.4** (Residual Witness)**.** _Let_ G=(_V,E_) _be an unweighted undirected graph with two designated terminals s and t, and G contains F as a flow subgraph. A tuple_ W=(_S,T,Y_) _is called a_ residual witness _of_ G _w.r.t F (or just residual witness for short) if the following conditions hold:_

1. (_S,T_) _is an s-t cut of_ G_<sub>F</sub> with value_ \(w_{\mathcal{G}_F}(S,T)\le k-k'-1\).<tbc>

_2._ \(Y=E_{\mathcal{G}_F}(S,T)\cup X\)_, where_ \(X\subseteq(S\times T)\backslash E_{\mathcal{G}_F}(S,T)\) _is of size at most_ \(k-k'-1-w_{\mathcal{G}_F}(S,T)\).

Intuitively, each \((a,b)\in X\) represents a _currently non-existent_ unit-capacity undirected edge that cross the cut (_S,T_). The set _X_ then represents a _pre-allocated_ set of edges that could potentially be added to G in the future, ensuring that the cut value of (_S,T_) remains at most \(k-k'-1\). Note unlike the previous definition of witness, it is possible to have \(X=\emptyset\).

**Invariant C.5** (Residual Witness Invariant)**.** _For any_ G _containing F as a flow subgraph, we have_ \(\nu(\mathcal{G})\ge f-k'\) _if and only if_ \(\mathcal{W}_F(\mathcal{G})=\emptyset\).

_Proof._ First, suppose that \(\nu(\mathcal{G})\ge f-k'\). Assume for the sake of contradiction that a residual witness exists and let (_S,T_) be a cut with respect to that witness. By definition of a witness, the cut (_S,T_) has value \(w_{\mathcal{G}_F}(S,T)\le k-k'-1\). Via Claim 3.1, we have \(|E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)|=\nu(F)+w_{\mathcal{G}_F}(S,T)\). Thus, we derive:

\(f-k'\le\nu(\mathcal{G})\le|E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)|=\nu(F)+w_{\mathcal{G}_F}(S,T)\le(f-k)+(k-k'-1)=f-k'-1\)

yielding a contradiction. This concludes \(\mathcal{W}_F(\mathcal{G})=\emptyset\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\nu(\mathcal{G})\le f-k'-1\). Let (_S,T_) be a minimum _s-t_ cut of G with value \(|E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)|=\nu(G)\le f-k'-1\). Again, following Claim 3.1, we have

\(w_{\mathcal{G}_F}(S,T)=|E_\mathcal{G}(S,T)|-\nu(F)\le(f-k'-1)-(f-k)=k-k'-1.\)
